transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, what made me come in is that I just keep feeling like I've ruined things for everybody. I'm in a plumbing apprenticeship right now, and I just feel like a total fake. Like I'm letting my family down, and the younger apprentices too, over stuff that... I don't know, I know other people would probably just fix it and move on from. But it's just really been weighing on me lately.
How long have you been feeling this way—like you're letting people down and feeling like a fake?
I'd say it's been about nine months now. Um, I tried to just deal with it for a while, but... yeah, it became a lot harder to hide once my work and my classes started slipping.
Over these past nine months, have you noticed feeling sad, down, or empty for most of the day, nearly every day?

Um, not really sad or empty, no. It's not like I'm crying all the time or feeling down in that way. It's more just... like I said, feeling like a failure. Just really guilty about messing things up and letting people down. But I wouldn't say I feel sad for most of the day.

Would you say you've always been the type of person who sets extremely high standards for yourself and has a hard time delegating tasks or accepting anything less than perfect, even before these last nine months?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I always want to do a good job, especially as an apprentice, but I wouldn't say I've ever been a perfectionist. Before all this started, I was pretty normal about my work. I didn't stress over every little detail or have a hard time letting other people do things. It's really just been these last nine months where I feel so guilty about every little mistake I make.
Did anything specific happen around nine months ago—like starting the apprenticeship, a change at work, or some other event—that seemed to trigger these feelings of guilt and failure?

Um, no, not really. I mean, the apprenticeship was already going on for a bit before this started. I can't really think of any big event or change that set it off. It just sort of... started happening.
Over these past nine months, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy?

Yeah, actually. I used to really like drawing, playing volleyball, and doing this volunteer stuff... but lately, I just don't care about any of it. I can walk right past my sketchbook or ignore texts from the volunteer group, and I just don't feel much of anything. It's weird because those things used to make me feel like myself, but now I just skip them.
Over these past nine months, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—like trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual?

Yeah, my sleep has definitely changed. Um, for a while there, I was getting by on just three or four hours a night, and I'd still show up totally wired for the job and my classes. But now... now it's different. I either can't fall asleep at all, or I wake up way before my alarm goes off, and I just feel like I never even rested.

During that time when you were only sleeping three or four hours but still felt wired and full of energy, did you also notice your mood being unusually elevated, more talkative than usual, or having racing thoughts or grand ideas?

Yeah, I did. Um, there were a few weeks back then where I felt almost too good. Like, I just felt like Miami was mine, you know? But at the same time, I was getting really annoyed easily. Like, if a coworker was slowing me down on a job, I would snap at them way harder than I normally would. It was just... I had all this energy and zero patience for anyone who couldn't keep up with me.

latest_inference.note: The patient's history of a distinct period with elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity ('Miami was mine'), increased irritability, and reduced patience—now followed by a depressive episode with anhedonia, guilt, and sleep disturbance—fits a hypomanic episode followed by major depressive episode, consistent with Bipolar II Disorder. This rules out unipolar MDD (F32.9) and persistent depressive disorder (F34.1), which do not account for the hypomanic symptoms.
